solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Line advanced ahead of call for attack (4,3)

indicatorNotes.ahead of: the first pieces come before SHOUT in the answer

blocks.note: A = advanced, as in A level

annotation.surface: A line of troops moves forward just before the order to charge is given.
annotation.walkthrough: The military surface makes 'attack' look like part of the story, but it stands alone as the verb: to lash out is to attack.
annotation.definitionFit: To lash out is to attack suddenly, physically or verbally.

entries.clue: Regularly play-acted — Greek character sent up in school (6)

indicatorNotes.Regularly: take every other letter, at regular intervals
indicatorNotes.sent up: in a down clue, sending something up turns it bottom to top

blocks.note: mu is a letter of the Greek alphabet

annotation.surface: Someone half-heartedly performing, with a Greek figure mocked in a school play.
annotation.walkthrough: The dash suggests a stage scene, but 'play-acted' is only a store of letters. The Lyceum was Aristotle's school in Athens, so the Greek flavour carries into the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: A lyceum is a school, after Aristotle's Lyceum; the word names secondary schools in several countries.

entries.clue: Grabbing the bananas, Italian breaks up for his lunch? (9)

indicatorNotes.Grabbing: the outer letters take hold of the inner ones
indicatorNotes.bananas: bananas = crazy, so the letters are scrambled
indicatorNotes.up: in a down clue, 'up' reads the letters bottom to top

annotation.surface: An Italian with a bunch of bananas takes a break for lunch.
annotation.walkthrough: IT + GAPS runs upward to SPAGTI, which then grabs HET. The question mark flags the definition as an example: pasta is what the stereotyped Italian of the surface eats.
annotation.definitionFit: Spaghetti is offered as a typical Italian's lunch, hence the question mark.

entries.clue: First to leave country departs on strange, crude vessel (3,4)

indicatorNotes.First to leave: the first letter of the word departs
indicatorNotes.on: in a down clue, D sits on top of RUM

blocks.note: soil = country (the land), minus its first letter
D = departs, as on a timetable

annotation.surface: An emigrant is the first to leave, sailing off in a strange, rough-built boat.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Crude vessel' reads as a primitive boat, but crude here is crude oil and the vessel is its container. 'Rum' for strange is old British slang.
annotation.definitionFit: Crude means unrefined petroleum here, and the steel barrels it is stored and shipped in are the vessels meant.

entries.clue: Colossus almost crushing stronghold — time for retaliation? (3,3,3)

indicatorNotes.almost: almost the whole word means stopping just short of its end, so the last letter goes
indicatorNotes.crushing: the outer word squeezes the inner one

blocks.note: TITAN, a colossus, without its last letter

annotation.surface: A giant flattening a fortress: surely payback time.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Time for retaliation' reads as one phrase, but 'time' gives the final T and 'for' is part of the wordplay's FORT, not a link.
annotation.definitionFit: Tit for tat is retaliation in kind, blow for blow.

entries.clue: Loose bit with nut and washer (4,3)

indicatorNotes.Loose: the letters are set loose and rearranged

annotation.surface: A loose drill bit, a nut and a washer rattling around a toolbox.
annotation.walkthrough: Nut and washer make the hardware kind of washer seem certain. A twin tub is an older British washing machine with separate tubs for washing and spinning.
annotation.definitionFit: Washer here means a washing machine, and this older British model has two drums, one for washing and one for spinning.

entries.clue: Trail originally joins wide river going north — one that crosses the border (5)

indicatorNotes.originally: what a word is originally is how it starts, so its first letter
indicatorNotes.joins: the pieces are put side by side
indicatorNotes.going north: in a down clue, north is upward, so DEE reads bottom to top

blocks.note: W = wide, as in cricket scoring
the Dee, a river in Scotland and in Wales

annotation.surface: A trail meets a broad river flowing north, and someone crosses into another country.
annotation.walkthrough: The Tweed is a river forming part of the border between England and Scotland; the definition teases because a river, not a traveller, is what does the crossing.
annotation.definitionFit: The River Tweed runs along the England–Scotland border, crossing it near Berwick.

entries.clue: Second son breaks new tin soldier (7)

indicatorNotes.breaks: S breaks into the middle of the other letters
indicatorNotes.new: the letters are made new, rearranged

annotation.surface: A younger son snaps his brother's new tin soldier.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Second son' reads as one phrase, but 'Second' is the definition, a moment. Soldier = ANT is a crossword staple, from soldier ants.
annotation.definitionFit: An instant is a second, a very short moment.

entries.clue: Beat with tail of wet fish (5)

indicatorNotes.tail of: a tail comes at the back end, so the word's last letter

annotation.surface: Hitting someone with a wet fish, a classic slapstick move.
annotation.walkthrough: ROUT comes first in the clue but second in the answer: 'with' lets the pieces join in either order.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain example of the class: a speckled freshwater species prized by anglers.

entries.clue: Slope above sunken track concealing quiet ruin (8)

indicatorNotes.above: in a down clue, BANK sits above the rest
indicatorNotes.concealing: to conceal something is to hide it inside, so the track's letters wrap round the quiet one

blocks.note: a rut is a groove worn in a track

annotation.surface: A slope above an old sunken lane hides a crumbling ruin.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Ruin' looks like a noun, a crumbling building, but it is the verb: to bankrupt someone is to ruin them.
annotation.definitionFit: To bankrupt a person or firm is to ruin them financially.

entries.clue: Rachel’s sick having eaten too much dessert (9)

indicatorNotes.having eaten: the outer letters take the inner ones in

blocks.note: OTT = over the top, too much

annotation.surface: Rachel feels ill after overeating at pudding time.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a coherent little story, with 'dessert' right where the overeating happened. A charlotte is a pudding of fruit or cream in a case of bread or sponge fingers.
annotation.definitionFit: A charlotte is a dessert, such as apple charlotte or charlotte russe.

entries.clue: Televised broadcast involves hospital (5)

indicatorNotes.involves: to involve is literally to roll something in, so the broadcast word wraps round the hospital letter

blocks.note: seed broadcast is sown, scattered widely

annotation.surface: A television programme features a hospital, like any medical drama.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast' seems to belong with 'Televised', but here it is the farming sense: scattering seed by hand.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the past participle: a programme that went out on air was displayed to viewers.

entries.clue: What’s making a comeback right after Universal show? (5)

indicatorNotes.making a comeback: the letters come back, right to left
indicatorNotes.after: R comes after the reversed letters

annotation.surface: A question about which Universal Pictures film is being revived.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Show' is the verb, as in show someone to their seat. 'Universal show' looks like a film title, but it splits: U belongs to the wordplay and 'show' is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Both verbs mean guiding a person along, as a cinema attendant leads guests to their seats.

entries.clue: Perhaps da Vinci’s structure on ship, more advanced externally (3,6)

indicatorNotes.externally: OLDER sits on the outside of MAST

blocks.note: a mast stands up from a ship's deck

annotation.surface: A claim that Leonardo designed a structure for a ship more sophisticated than its time.
annotation.walkthrough: 'More advanced' suggests technology, but here it means advanced in age. 'Perhaps' warns that Leonardo is just one example of the class.
annotation.definitionFit: Leonardo da Vinci is an old master, a great European painter before about 1800.

entries.clue: Dressing to impress, hugging mother, heading for town, fine and happy (6,7)

indicatorNotes.hugging: TO ETCH wraps round the middle pieces
indicatorNotes.heading for: the heading of a word is its top, so its first letter

blocks.note: TO + ETCH; to etch is to impress a design

annotation.surface: Someone dresses up smartly, hugs their mum and heads into town in a cheerful mood.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Dressing to impress' is a set phrase about clothes, but it splits: the dressing is a sauce, and 'to impress' is the word 'to' plus a verb for engraving.
annotation.definitionFit: Tomato ketchup is a sauce, and a dressing is a sauce put on food.

entries.clue: Sign up cook for grand event, initially tense (5-4)

indicatorNotes.up: in a down clue, 'up' reads INK bottom to top
indicatorNotes.initially: initially means at the start, so only the first letter of event

blocks.note: to ink a contract is to sign it
to cook for people is to feed them

annotation.surface: Someone agrees to cater a big occasion and is nervous from the start.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sign up' looks like enlisting, but it splits: INK is the sign and 'up' reverses it. Likewise 'for' belongs with 'cook', not with 'grand event'.
annotation.definitionFit: A knife-edge situation is a tense one, balanced on a fine line.

entries.clue: Stop around middle of Derby, mainly to have food and drink (6,3)

indicatorNotes.around: HALT goes round the inserted letters
indicatorNotes.middle of: the middle of a word is what is left when both ends are trimmed away
indicatorNotes.mainly: most of the word, so drop its last letter

blocks.note: EAT, a word for having food, cut short by 'mainly'

annotation.surface: A pit stop at the Derby, the famous horse race, mostly for a bite and a drink.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Food and drink' reads as one pair, but 'food' belongs to the wordplay (EAT) and 'drink' alone is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Herbal tea is a drink infused from herbs rather than tea leaves.

entries.clue: Special cap limits extreme cracking (8)

indicatorNotes.limits: LID forms the limits, the outside, of END

blocks.note: the extreme of something is its end

annotation.surface: A special cap that limits extreme cracking, perhaps on a pipe or a jar.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cracking' sits at the end where it looks like breakage, but it is the British praise word: a cracking game is a splendid one.
annotation.definitionFit: Cracking is British informal for excellent, which is what splendid means.

entries.clue: One’s clutched by awful tourist — it might be necessary to remove coat (5,8)

annotation.definition: it might be necessary to remove coat

indicatorNotes.clutched by: something clutched is gripped tightly, held inside another's grasp

blocks.note: pants = rubbish, awful, in British slang
a tripper is a day tourist

annotation.surface: A dreadful tourist grabs someone, perhaps in a crowd, who has to take off a coat.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Awful tourist' reads as one phrase, but it splits into two words; 'pants' as British slang for rubbish is the one to know. The coat is not clothing but a layer of paint.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by function: this solvent softens old layers on doors and furniture so they can be scraped away.

entries.clue: Got upset about old money in part of London (7)

indicatorNotes.upset: in a down clue, upset turns GOT upside down
indicatorNotes.about: TOG goes round the other letters

annotation.surface: Someone upset about their old savings somewhere in London.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Old money' suggests pre-decimal British coins, but it splits into O and TIN. Tooting is a district of south London.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: this district lies in the borough of Wandsworth, south of the Thames.

entries.clue: Nationalist parade’s beginning at one following resistance to uprising (7)

indicatorNotes.beginning: a word's beginning is where it starts, its first letter
indicatorNotes.following: to follow is to come after, so one is placed after resistance
indicatorNotes.uprising: in a down clue, rising reads TO bottom to top

annotation.surface: A nationalist march starts off a resistance movement's revolt.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Uprising' looks like a noun meaning revolt, and RIOT is even visible in the answer, but it only turns TO upward.
annotation.definitionFit: A patriot is a nationalist, someone devoted to their country.

entries.clue: Reeves losing head in training is possible cause of violent reaction (6)

indicatorNotes.losing head: a word that loses its head loses its top, its first letter
indicatorNotes.in: the beheaded name sits in the middle of the training abbreviation

blocks.note: KEANU, the actor Keanu Reeves, without his first letter

annotation.surface: Keanu Reeves, frustrated in training, might explain a violent outburst.
annotation.walkthrough: The violent reaction sounds like an action-film fight, but it is an allergic reaction. The surname stands for the first name Keanu.
annotation.definitionFit: Peanuts are a well-known cause of severe allergic reactions.

entries.clue: Fold plastic once, retaining length of course (9)

indicatorNotes.plastic: plastic = mouldable, so the letters are reshaped

annotation.surface: Instructions for folding a plastic sheet once while keeping the length of a course.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fold' looks like a verb for creasing plastic, but it is the noun: a sheep fold.
annotation.definitionFit: A farming sense: a fold is a fenced pen where sheep are kept, the root of 'sheepfold'.

entries.clue: Current over limit at first in live wire (5)

indicatorNotes.over: in a down clue, 'over' turns AC upside down
indicatorNotes.at first: at first means at the start, so only the opening letter of limit
indicatorNotes.in: the limit letter is placed in the middle of the word for live

annotation.surface: A warning about current exceeding the limit in a live wire.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Live wire' is a single electrical phrase, but it splits: 'live' is BE and 'wire' alone is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A cable is an insulated wire for carrying current.

entries.clue: Colour of flower, as Miss Doolittle might once have called it? (5)

indicators: as Miss Doolittle might once have called it

indicatorNotes.as Miss Doolittle might once have called: Eliza Doolittle in Pygmalion, before her lessons, dropped her aitches

blocks.note: a flower is a river, something that flows; the Humber, in northern England

blocks.clueFragment: as Miss Doolittle might once have called it
blocks.note: with the H dropped, Cockney style

annotation.surface: A question about what Eliza Doolittle would have called a flower's colour.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Flower' is the crossword river, a thing that flows. Eliza Doolittle, the Cockney flower seller of Pygmalion and My Fair Lady, dropped her aitches before her elocution lessons.
annotation.definitionFit: Umber is a brown earth pigment and the colour named after it.

entries.clue: Rag, as in something used when driving? (5)

indicatorNotes.as in: the answer is said the same as the thing described

blocks.note: golf tees hold the ball for a drive

annotation.surface: A cloth rag, perhaps kept in the car for use on the road.
annotation.walkthrough: The driving is golf, not motoring: a drive is a long shot off the tee. 'Rag' is the verb meaning to tease.
annotation.definitionFit: Rag is British slang for mocking playfully, as students rag a friend; both verbs mean poking fun.

entries.clue: City’s name associated with smart technology? (5)

annotation.surface: A city whose name has become a byword for smart, high-tech living.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is fair on its own terms, since Dubai markets itself as a smart city; 'name' is a verb here.
annotation.definitionFit: Dubai is a city in the United Arab Emirates.

entries.clue: Wrong day to cover international sport (9)

indicatorNotes.to cover: MON covers INT, holding it inside

annotation.surface: Someone picked the wrong day to report on an international sporting fixture.
annotation.walkthrough: 'International sport' reads as one phrase, but 'international' belongs to the wordplay, leaving 'sport' alone as the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Badminton is a racket sport played with a shuttlecock.

entries.clue: Wine, say, knocked back aboard physician’s boat (7)

indicatorNotes.knocked back: EG is turned back to front
indicatorNotes.aboard: the letters go on board, inside DR

annotation.surface: Wine downed on board a doctor's yacht.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Knocked back' sounds like drinking the wine, but it reverses only EG. A dredger is a boat that scoops mud from riverbeds.
annotation.definitionFit: A dredger is a boat fitted to dredge silt from waterways.

entries.clue: Opponent ran towards boxing competitor (7)

indicatorNotes.boxing: the words box the answer, holding it inside

annotation.surface: A boxer's opponent rushes across the ring at a rival.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Boxing' fits the fight scene too well to look like an indicator, but it tells you the answer is boxed inside the first three words.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: anyone who signs up to take part in a race or tournament is one.
